title: Polymerisation
overview: Understand condensation polymers in depth, predict monomers from a repeat unit, and consider polymer degradability. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Explain addition and condensation polymerisation and identify repeat units.
Deduce monomers from polyester and polyamide repeat units.
Describe polymer hydrolysis and relate structure to degradability.
Evaluate disposal, recycling and environmental impacts using chemical reasoning.

definitions.definition: Joining unsaturated monomers without eliminating a small molecule.
Joining bifunctional monomers while eliminating a small molecule such as H₂O or HCl.
The smallest structural section that repeats along a polymer chain.
Capable of breakdown by biological action under suitable conditions.

sections.title: Addition versus condensation
content: Addition polymers come from C=C monomers and their repeat units contain only atoms from the monomer. Condensation polymers need two functional groups per monomer; each link forms with loss of a small molecule. Name the link and show open bonds through repeat-unit brackets.
bullets: The repeat unit must preserve chain connectivity.
Do not include n copies of a small-molecule by-product inside the repeat unit.

sections.title: Polyesters
content: A diol plus a dicarboxylic acid forms –O–C(=O)– ester links with water loss; a diol plus a diacyl chloride can form the same links with HCl loss. Hydrolysis cleaves the ester link under acidic or alkaline conditions.
bullets: Cut the repeat unit through ester links to recover both bifunctional monomers.
Under alkaline hydrolysis, carboxylate salts form before acidification.

sections.title: Polyamides and peptides
content: A diamine plus a dicarboxylic acid/diacyl chloride forms –NH–C(=O)– links. Amino acids can self-condense into polypeptides. Hydrolysis breaks amide links but generally needs stronger conditions than ester hydrolysis.
bullets: Restore –NH₂ and –COOH at the cut bonds when deducing monomers.
Account for protonation state under acidic/alkaline hydrolysis.

sections.title: Properties and sustainability
content: Condensation polymers containing hydrolysable links can be more degradable than C–C addition polymers, but real biodegradation depends on crystallinity, access, temperature and enzymes. Evaluate reuse, mechanical/chemical recycling, feedstock and energy use instead of assuming one disposal route is always best.
bullets: Biodegradable does not mean instant breakdown everywhere.
Link a property claim to a named structural feature.

examTips: Mark the exact link before drawing monomers or hydrolysis products.
Show two continuation bonds through every repeat-unit bracket.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Leaving a C=C bond in an addition-polymer repeat unit.
Cutting the wrong bond when deducing condensation monomers.
Calling every condensation polymer readily biodegradable.

quickRecall.question: What feature identifies a polyester?
quickRecall.answer: Repeated ester links, –COO–, in the main chain.

quickRecall.question: How are monomers recovered from a polyamide repeat unit?
quickRecall.answer: Cut the C(=O)–N links and restore –COOH/acid-derivative and –NH₂ ends.

quickRecall.question: Why can condensation polymers be hydrolysed?
quickRecall.answer: Their ester or amide links can react with water under suitable acid/base conditions.

quickRecall.question: Does biodegradable mean harmless or instantly decomposed?
quickRecall.answer: No; breakdown depends on environment and products, so conditions and life-cycle effects matter.
